    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/parkinsonsdisease.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">Disease</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Paralysis Agitans</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Shaking Palsy</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> (PD) is a type of movement disorder. It happens when nerve cells in the brain don't produce enough of a brain chemical called dopamine. Sometimes it is genetic, but most cases do not seem to run in families. Exposure to chemicals in the environment might play a role.</p><p>Symptoms begin gradually, often on one side of the body.  Later they affect both sides. They  include:</p><ul><li>Trembling of hands, arms, legs, jaw and face </li><li>Stiffness of the arms, legs and trunk </li><li>Slowness of movement </li><li>Poor balance and coordination </li></ul><p>As symptoms get worse, people with the <span class="qt1">disease</span> may have trouble walking, talking, or doing simple tasks. They may also have problems such as depression, sleep problems, or trouble chewing, swallowing, or speaking.</p><p>There is no specific test for PD, so it can be difficult to diagnose.  Doctors use a medical history and a neurological examination to diagnose it.</p><p>PD usually begins around age 60, but it can start earlier. It is more common in men than in women. There is no cure for PD. A variety of medicines sometimes help symptoms dramatically. Surgery and deep brain stimulation (DBS) can help severe cases. With DBS, electrodes are surgically implanted in the brain. They send electrical pulses to stimulate the parts of the brain that control movement.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke</p></content>

    <document rank="0" url="https://medlineplus.gov/lewybodydementia.html">
      <content name="title">Lewy Body Dementia</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dementia with Lewy Bodies</content>
      <content name="altTitle">LBD</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Lewy body <span class="qt1">disease</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> dementia</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is Lewy body dementia (LBD)?<p>Lewy body dementia (LBD) is one of the most common types of dementia in older adults. Dementia is a loss of mental functions that is severe enough to affect your daily life and activities. These functions include:</p><ul><li>Memory</li><li>Language skills</li><li>Visual perception (your ability to make sense of what you see)</li><li>Problem solving</li><li>Trouble with everyday tasks</li><li>The ability to focus and pay attention</li></ul>What are the types of Lewy body dementia (LBD)?<p>There are two types of LBD: dementia with Lewy bodies and <span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> dementia.</p><p>Both types cause the same changes in the brain. And, over time, they can cause similar symptoms. The main difference is in when the cognitive (thinking) and movement symptoms start.</p><p>Dementia with Lewy bodies causes problems with thinking ability that seem similar to Alzheimer's <span class="qt1">disease</span>. Later, it also causes other symptoms, such as movement symptoms, visual hallucinations, and certain sleep disorders. It also causes more trouble with mental activities than with memory.</p><p><span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> dementia starts as a movement disorder. It first causes the symptoms of <span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>: slowed movement, muscle stiffness, tremor, and a shuffling walk. Later on, it causes dementia.</p>What causes Lewy body dementia (LBD)?<p>LBD happens when Lewy bodies build up in parts of the brain that control memory, thinking, and movement.  Lewy bodies are abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein. Researchers don't know exactly why these deposits form. But they do know that other <span class="qt1">diseases</span>, such as <span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>, also involve a build-up of that protein.</p>Who is at risk for Lewy body dementia (LBD)?<p>The biggest risk factor for LBD is age; most people who get it are over age 50. People who have a family history of LBD are also at higher risk.</p>What are the symptoms of Lewy body dementia (LBD)?<p>LBD is a progressive <span class="qt1">disease</span>. This means that the symptoms start slowly and get worse over time. The most common symptoms include changes in cognition, movement, sleep, and behavior:</p><ul><li>Dementia, which is a loss of mental functions that is severe enough to affect your daily life and activities</li><li>Changes in concentration, attention, alertness, and wakefulness. These changes usually happen from day to day. But sometimes they can also happen throughout the same day.</li><li>Visual hallucinations, which means seeing things that are not there</li><li>Problems with movement and posture, including slowness of movement, difficulty walking, and muscle stiffness. These are called <span class="qt0">parkinsonian</span> motor symptoms.</li><li>REM sleep behavior disorder, a condition in which a person seems to act out dreams. It may include vivid dreaming, talking in one's sleep, violent movements, or falling out of bed. This may be the earliest symptom of LBD in some people. It can appear several years before any other LBD symptoms.</li><li>Changes in behavior and mood, such as depression, anxiety, and apathy (a lack of interest in normal daily activities or events)</li></ul><p>In the early stages of LBD, symptoms can be mild, and people can function fairly normally. As the <span class="qt1">disease</span> gets worse, people with LBD need more help due to problems with thinking and movement. In the later stages of the <span class="qt1">disease</span>, they often cannot care for themselves.</p>How is Lewy body dementia (LBD) diagnosed?<p>There isn't one test that can diagnose LBD. It is important to see an experienced doctor to get a diagnosis. This would usually be a specialist such as a neurologist. The doctor will:</p><ul><li>Do a medical history, including taking a detailed account of the symptoms. The doctor will talk to both the patient and caregivers.</li><li>Do physical and neurological exams</li><li>Do tests to rule out other conditions that could cause similar symptoms. These could include blood tests and brain imaging tests.</li><li>Do neuropsychological tests to evaluate memory and other cognitive functions</li></ul><p>LBD can be hard to diagnose, because <span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> and Alzheimer's <span class="qt1">disease</span> cause similar symptoms. Scientists think that Lewy body <span class="qt1">disease</span> might be related to these <span class="qt1">diseases</span>, or that they sometimes happen together.</p><p>It's also important to know which type of LBD a person has, so the doctor can treat that type's particular symptoms. It also helps the doctor understand how the <span class="qt1">disease</span> will affect the person over time. The doctor makes a diagnosis based on when certain symptoms start:</p><ul><li>If cognitive symptoms start within a year of movement problems, the diagnosis is dementia with Lewy bodies</li><li>If cognitive problems start more than a year after the movement problems, the diagnosis is <span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> dementia</li></ul>What are the treatments for Lewy body dementia (LBD)?<p>There is no cure for LBD, but treatments can help with the symptoms:</p><ul><li>Medicines may help with some of the cognitive, movement, and psychiatric symptoms</li><li>Physical therapy can help with movement problems</li><li>Occupational therapy may help find ways to more easily do everyday activities</li><li>Speech therapy may help with swallowing difficulties and trouble speaking loudly and clearly</li><li>Mental health counseling can help people with LBD and their families learn how to manage difficult emotions and behaviors. It can also help them plan for the future.</li><li>Music or art therapy may reduce anxiety and improve well-being</li></ul><p>Support groups can also be helpful for people with LBD and their caregivers. Support groups can give emotional and social support. They are also a place where people can share tips about how to deal with day-to-day challenges.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/movementdisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Movement Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ataxia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Chorea</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dyskinesia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Tardive Dyskinesia</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Movement disorders are neurologic conditions that cause problems with movement, such as:</p><ul><li>Increased movement that can be voluntary (intentional) or involuntary (unintended)</li><li>Decreased or slow voluntary movement</li></ul><p>There are many different movement disorders. Some of the more common types include:</p><ul><li>Ataxia, the loss of muscle coordination</li><li>Dystonia, in which involuntary contractions of your muscles cause twisting and repetitive movements. The movements can be painful.</li><li>Huntington's <span class="qt1">disease</span>, an inherited <span class="qt1">disease</span> that causes nerve cells in certain parts of the brain to waste away. This includes the nerve cells that help to control voluntary movement.</li><li><span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>, which is a disorder that slowly gets worse over time. It causes tremors, slowness of movement, and trouble walking.</li><li>Tourette syndrome, a condition that causes people to make sudden twitches, movements, or sounds (tics)</li><li>Tremor and essential tremor, which cause involuntary trembling or shaking movements. The movements may be in one or more parts of your body.</li></ul><p>Causes of movement disorders include:</p><ul><li>Genetics</li><li>Infections</li><li>Medicines</li><li>Damage to the brain, spinal cord, or peripheral nerves</li><li>Metabolic disorders</li><li>Stroke and vascular <span class="qt1">diseases</span></li><li>Toxins</li></ul><p>Treatment varies by disorder. Medicines can cure some disorders. Others get better when an underlying <span class="qt1">disease</span> is treated. Often, however, there is no cure. In that case, the goal of treatment is to improve symptoms and relieve pain.</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/tremor.html">
      <content name="title">Tremor</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Essential Tremor</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is a tremor?<p>A tremor is a neurological condition that includes shaking or trembling movements in one or more parts of your body. It most often affects the hands. But it can also affect the arms, legs, head, vocal cords, and torso (trunk). A tremor is involuntary, meaning that you cannot control it. It happens because of muscle contractions.</p><p>A tremor may come and go, or it may be constant. It can happen on its own or be caused by another disorder. It is not life threatening, but it may cause challenges. It can make it hard to do daily life tasks such as writing, typing, eating, and dressing. In some cases, a tremor can even lead to disabilities.</p>What are the types of tremor?<p>There are several types of tremor, including:</p><ul><li>Essential tremor, sometimes called benign essential tremor or familial tremor. This is the most common type. It usually affects both your hands and arms while you are moving them. It can also affect your head, voice, or legs. </li><li><span class="qt0">Parkinsonian</span> tremor, which is a common symptom in people who have <span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>. It usually affects one or both hands when they are at rest, but it can affect the chin, lips, face, and legs.</li><li>Dystonic tremor, which happens in people who have dystonia. Dystonia is a movement disorder in which you have involuntary muscle contractions. The contractions cause you to have twisting and repetitive movements. It can affect any muscle in the body.</li></ul>What causes tremor?<p>Generally, tremor is caused by a problem in the deep parts of the brain that control movements. For most types, the cause is unknown. Some types are inherited and run in families. There can also be other causes, such as:</p><ul><li>Neurologic disorders, including multiple sclerosis, <span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>, stroke, and traumatic brain injury</li><li>Certain medicines, such as asthma medicines, chemotherapy, corticosteroids, and medicines used for certain psychiatric and neurological disorders</li><li>Alcohol use disorder (AUD) or alcohol withdrawal</li><li>Poisoning from certain toxic substances, including pesticides and heavy metals such as mercury and lead</li><li>Hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid)</li><li>Liver or kidney failure</li><li>Anxiety or panic</li><li>Too much caffeine</li></ul>Who is at risk for tremor?<p>Anyone can get tremor, but it is most common in middle-aged and older adults. For certain types of tremor, having a family history raises your risk of getting it.</p>What are the symptoms of tremor?<p>Symptoms of tremor may include:</p><ul><li>Rhythmic shaking in the hands, arms, head, legs, or torso</li><li>Shaky voice</li><li>Difficulty writing or drawing</li><li>Problems holding and controlling utensils, such as a spoon</li></ul>How is tremor diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms </li><li>A physical exam, which includes checking:
		<ul><li>Whether the tremor happens when the muscles are at rest or in action</li><li>The location of the tremor</li><li>How often you have the tremor and how strong it is</li></ul>
</li><li>A neurological exam, including checking for:
		<ul><li>Problems with balance</li><li>Problems with speech</li><li>Increased muscle stiffness</li></ul>
</li><li>Blood or urine tests to look for the cause</li><li>Imaging tests to help figure out if the cause is damage to your brain</li><li>Tests that check your abilities to do daily tasks such as handwriting and holding a fork or cup</li><li>An electromyogram, a test that measures involuntary muscle activity and how your muscles respond to nerve stimulation</li></ul>What are the treatments for tremor?<p>There is no cure for most forms of tremor, but there are treatments to help manage symptoms. In some cases, the symptoms may be so mild that you do not need treatment.</p><p>Finding the right treatment depends on getting the right diagnosis of the cause. Tremor caused by another medical condition may get better or go away when you treat that condition. If your tremor is caused by a certain medicine, stopping that medicine usually makes the tremor go away.</p><p>Treatments for tremor can include:</p><ul><li>Medicines. There are different medicines for the specific types of tremor. Another option is Botox injections, which can treat several different types of tremor.</li><li>Surgery may be used for severe cases that do not get better with medicines. The most common type is deep brain stimulation (DBS). DBS uses electrodes that are implanted in the brain. The electrodes send electrical pulses to the parts of the brain that are causing the tremor.</li><li>Physical, speech-language, and occupational therapy, which may help to control tremor and deal with the daily challenges caused by the tremor.</li></ul><p>If you find that caffeine and other stimulants trigger your tremors, it may be helpful to cut them from your diet.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/degenerativenervediseases.html">
      <content name="title">Degenerative Nerve <span class="qt1">Diseases</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ataxia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Neurodegenerative <span class="qt1">Diseases</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Prion <span class="qt1">Diseases</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Degenerative nerve <span class="qt1">diseases</span> affect many of your body's activities, such as balance, movement, talking, breathing, and heart function.   Many of these <span class="qt1">diseases</span> are genetic. Sometimes the cause is a medical condition such as alcoholism, a tumor, or a stroke. Other causes may include toxins, chemicals, and viruses.  Sometimes the cause is unknown.</p><p>Degenerative nerve <span class="qt1">diseases</span> include:</p><ul><li>Alzheimer's <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li>Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis</li><li>Friedreich ataxia</li><li>Huntington's <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li>Lewy body <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li><span class="qt0">Parkinson</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li>Spinal muscular atrophy</li></ul><p>Degenerative nerve <span class="qt1">diseases</span> can be serious or life-threatening. It depends on the type. Most of them have no cure. Treatments may help improve symptoms, relieve pain, and increase mobility.</p></content>
